flows.title: Answer a question with evidence
flows.subtitle: From a bare question to a cited evidence pack: log searches, register sources, file claims, catch a contradiction, resolve it, and audit the result.

steps.title: Open the research ledger
steps.explain: Every research session starts by declaring the topic, the sub-question, the entities being compared and the fields we care about. This also resets any previous research ledger, so the run is reproducible.
argv: Which local database engine handles concurrent analytics better: DuckDB or SQLite?
How does each engine handle concurrent readers and writers?

steps.title: Log the first search
steps.explain: Queries are logged against a budget before they are run, so the session cannot silently turn into endless scrolling. Each distinct query counts once.

steps.title: Register a primary source (DuckDB docs)
steps.explain: A claim is only as good as its source, so sources are registered first with a verbatim excerpt. Later claims must quote this excerpt word for word to count as verified.
argv: DuckDB SQL constraints and transaction semantics
DuckDB serializes writes per table but allows concurrent readers during transactions.

steps.title: Register a second primary source (SQLite WAL)
steps.explain: The second side of the comparison gets its own primary source. Two independent primaries make the eventual matrix credible.
argv: WAL mode allows readers and one writer to proceed concurrently without blocking.

steps.title: File the first claim (verified)
steps.explain: A claim states one fact for one entity and field, backed by an exact quote. Because the quote appears verbatim in the stored excerpt, this claim lands as VERIFIED with HIGH confidence.
argv: DuckDB serializes writes per table while allowing concurrent readers
DuckDB serializes writes per table but allows concurrent readers during transactions.

steps.title: File the second claim (verified)
steps.explain: Same discipline for SQLite. Note the quote again matches the excerpt exactly — that is what keeps the confidence HIGH.
argv: SQLite in WAL mode allows one writer and many concurrent readers
WAL mode allows readers and one writer to proceed concurrently without blocking.

steps.title: File a contradictory claim
steps.explain: A blog post disagrees with the official DuckDB docs. It gets recorded too — but with LOW confidence and an unverified quote, because honesty about weak evidence is the point.
argv: A secondary blog claims DuckDB supports fully concurrent multi-writer transactions
DuckDB supports multiple concurrent writers without table locks

steps.title: Resolve the contradiction
steps.explain: Two claims now disagree about DuckDB. research-resolve declares the winner with a reason and marks the loser superseded, so no report can quietly cite the dead claim later.
argv: Primary DuckDB documentation overrides the secondary blog claim for the current release

steps.title: Record what could not be found
steps.explain: Nobody published crash-recovery benchmarks for these two engines. A gap records exactly that, with the query that was tried and why it failed — so 'unknown' is a documented fact, not a shrug.
argv: No public source compares crash recovery times between DuckDB and SQLite

steps.title: Score the sources
steps.explain: Before trusting the ledger, each source gets a quality score based on tier, publisher and freshness. Low scorers would be flagged here.

steps.title: Render the comparison matrix
steps.explain: The wide-table command turns the ledger into an entity-by-field matrix. Every cell shows its evidence state, so empty or contested cells are visible at a glance.

steps.title: Write the evidence pack
steps.explain: The session ends with a deliverable: a Markdown pack containing every usable claim with its citation and quote, every gap, and the resolution ruling — ready to hand to a writer or an agent.

steps.title: Audit the ledger
steps.explain: Finally the suite audits itself: dangling source references, high-confidence claims without verified quotes, and weak citations all fail here. A clean PASS is what makes the pack trustworthy.

flows.title: Ship a change safely
flows.subtitle: Specify the goal, make it testable, build the deliverable, verify it mechanically, put it through review, and hand the session over — the spec-driven delivery loop end to end.

steps.title: Write the spec
steps.explain: A change starts as a goal with user stories and explicit non-goals — not as code. The spec ledger is also the contract every later gate checks against.
argv: Ship a CSV export on the billing dashboard so finance can close the month without engineering help
As a finance user I want a CSV export so I can file invoices myself

steps.title: Make it testable
steps.explain: Each story gets acceptance criteria in Given / When / Then form. If a criterion cannot be written, the story is not ready to be built.
argv: the billing dashboard showing one month of invoices
a file downloads containing every invoice row for that month

steps.title: Add the implementing task
steps.explain: Tasks link back to the criterion they verify, so 'done' is a graph, not a feeling. Uncovered criteria get flagged by spec-check.
argv: Wire the export button to the CSV endpoint and add a regression test

steps.title: Build the deliverable
steps.explain: The work itself produces an artifact — here a delivery report instantiated from the artifact-studio template. An empty artifacts folder cannot pass verification.

steps.title: Check spec coverage
steps.explain: spec-check re-reads the ledger mechanically: every story has criteria, every criterion has a task, no dependency cycles, non-goals recorded.

steps.title: Verify the delivery
steps.explain: verify-delivery demands observable evidence: the artifact must exist (L1) and a real shell check must pass (L2). Claiming a level you did not reach fails the gate.

steps.title: Open a review
steps.explain: Mechanical verification says the artifact exists — it says nothing about quality. A review declares its target and focus, then records findings against them.

steps.title: Record a real finding
steps.explain: Reviewers log findings with a file, a line and a severity — not vibes. A MAJOR is correct code that will bite soon; a BLOCKING would fail the verdict outright.
argv: CSV fields are joined without quoting, so commas in company names break every row
Escape and quote fields per RFC 4180

steps.title: Render the verdict
steps.explain: The verdict is computed, not negotiated: BLOCKING findings force FAIL, MAJOR or MINOR yield PASS_WITH_FINDINGS. The report also records what was not reviewed.

steps.title: Hand the session over
steps.explain: Done or not, the session ends with a handoff pack: what was completed, what the next person must do, and the open finding — so nothing lives only in someone's head.
argv: Specified, built, verified and reviewed the billing CSV export end to end
Spec: 1 story, 1 acceptance criterion, 1 covering task
Delivery verified at L2 with a non-empty artifact
Fix the MAJOR CSV quoting finding before merging

flows.title: Chase a bug to its root cause
flows.subtitle: A real bug in the bundled demo project: record the case, read only the suspect file, falsify one hypothesis, confirm the next one, and write the report.

steps.title: Record the case
steps.explain: Debugging starts with discipline, not guesses: the symptom, the suspect file and a repro command are written down before anything is touched.
argv: Running the demo app with a non-numeric limit prints an empty list instead of an error

steps.title: Read the suspect file (scoped)
steps.explain: scope-read with --debug-scope only allows files registered as debug targets — no wandering through the whole repo. The read returns numbered lines and a checksum as evidence.

steps.title: Log hypothesis H1
steps.explain: A hypothesis is only valid if it predicts something checkable. H1 suspects the argument never reaches the program at all.
argv: The command line argument never reaches the program
The program behaves identically with and without an argument

steps.title: Falsify H1
steps.explain: The prediction fails: with 'abc' the program prints [] while with '3' it prints squares — so the argument clearly arrives. H1 is dead, and the ledger remembers why.
argv: Running with 'abc' prints [] while running with 3 prints squares — the argument clearly arrives

steps.title: Log hypothesis H2
steps.explain: Next suspect: the input parser itself. H2 predicts that calling int() on the bad value raises an error that something upstream swallows.
argv: parse_int swallows the ValueError and returns 0, so range(0) yields an empty list

steps.title: Confirm H2
steps.explain: The test raises exactly as predicted, and the scoped read shows the except-branch returning 0. H2 is confirmed — root cause found. (Two falsified hypotheses in a row would trip a circuit breaker and force escalation instead of more guessing.)
argv: int('abc') raises ValueError; app.py catches it and silently returns 0

steps.title: Write the report
steps.explain: The session closes with a root-cause report: what the fix was, what was deliberately not checked, and the confirmed hypothesis chain that justifies it.
argv: parse_int now re-raises ValueError instead of returning 0
Not exercised with negative or very large limits

flows.title: Make a call you won't regret
flows.subtitle: Frame an architecture question, score the options on a weighted matrix, and turn the outcome into a numbered ADR — the decision-review loop in three moves.

steps.title: Frame the question
steps.explain: Good decisions start with an honest intake: the question, the context, the hard constraints and — crucially — what is explicitly out of scope.
argv: Should the test console run commands against a shared demo workspace or isolated sandboxes per run?
The web console executes real workbench commands and must keep ledger state inspectable
Keep the Workspace tab able to show live ledgers

steps.title: Score the options
steps.explain: The seeded decision matrix weighs inspectability, effort and reversibility for three options. decision-score does the weighted math, ranks them, and writes the result JSON for the next step.

steps.title: Write the ADR
steps.explain: The ruling becomes an Architecture Decision Record: numbered, dated, owned, with the scored option table and a sensitivity analysis filled in from the result JSON. It even lists the sections a human still owes (context, consequences) — an ADR is a decision, not an essay.
argv: Run the test console against a shared demo workspace
